big_idea: When shapes are REARRANGED, the AREA stays the SAME. Decompose, rearrange, recompose.
learning_intention: We are learning to show area stays the same when parts are rearranged.
student_learning_goal: I can show area stays the same when parts are rearranged.
success_criteria: I can show AREA is the SAME.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Symmy and Flippy — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.

minds_on.hook: Flippy: I have 6 tiles. I make a rectangle — area = 6. Now I REARRANGE into an L-shape — STILL 6! Area stays the SAME! Flippy opens: 'Same TILES, SAME area — Flippy's rule!' Yesterday Symmy SORTED shapes — today we DECOMPOSE them.
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Symmy and Flippy puppets. 'Friends — yesterday sides and symmetry. Today COMPOSE, DECOMPOSE, and AREA CONSERVATION.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write COMPOSE, DECOMPOSE, AREA on chart. 'Compose = put together. Decompose = break apart. Area = how much space the inside covers.'

Demonstrate. Show 6 unit tiles. 'Make a 2×3 rectangle. Area = 6 tiles.' Rearrange. 'Now an L-shape with the same 6 tiles. Area = STILL 6.' Rearrange again. 'A long row of 6. Still 6.' Stack into a different L. 'Still 6!'

'Flippy says — REARRANGING the parts doesn't CHANGE the AREA. Same tiles, same area.'

More examples:
- 4 tiles → 2x2 square OR 1x4 row OR L-shape. All area = 4.
- 8 tiles → many arrangements. All area = 8.
- 12 tiles → 4x3 rectangle OR 6x2 OR plus-sign shape. All area = 12.

'Symmy says — COMPOSE = build. DECOMPOSE = break. AREA = inside space. The rule: REARRANGING never CHANGES area.'

Non-example. 'If I REMOVE a tile? Area DROPS by 1. So removing changes area, but rearranging doesn't.'

'Today we DECOMPOSE shapes and prove area stays the same.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: 6 tiles arranged 3 different ways. Count area each time.
Three stations. A: Decompose 4 shapes into pattern blocks. B: Rearrange 6 tiles into 3 different shapes. C: Pick a target shape, decompose, rearrange.
Stretch at C: rearrange 12 tiles into 4 different shapes.

steps.teacher_prompt: Show: same tiles → same area no matter the shape.

steps.instruction: STRATEGY COMPARE: Two pairs decompose a hexagon — Pair A into triangles, Pair B into a rectangle + two triangles. Class compares: same tiles? Same area? Cite Piagetian conservation + Battista (2007) area-as-count.
steps.teacher_prompt: Flippy: 'Different decompositions, SAME tiles, SAME area.'

differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Sentence frame: 'I rearranged ___ tiles. Area is still ___.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Children stand in 4-square arrangement, then rearrange to L-shape. Same children = same area.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: decomposes; rearranges; recognizes area unchanged.

discussion_prompts: Why does area stay the same when we rearrange?
consolidation.exit_routine: Flippy's refrain — class chants: 'Same TILES, SAME area — Flippy's rule!' (3x). Each child rearranges 6 tiles two ways and writes 'area = 6 in both'.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child says BIGGER LOOKING means MORE AREA — repairing the appearance-area conflation at Grade 2
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On area conservation, the trap is Piagetian conservation-of-area failure: child sees 6 tiles spread out and says 'more area' (Battista 2007 area-as-count vs perimeter conflation). Without conservation, Lesson 4 mapping and Lesson 5 capstone cannot ground.

Yesterday Symmy sorted shapes by attributes. Today we DECOMPOSE and rearrange — area stays SAME because tile count stays SAME. Lesson 3 congruence; Lesson 4 maps; Lesson 5 capstones.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair at B. Child has 6 tiles in 2 arrangements: rectangle (compact) and L-shape (spread out). Says 'L-shape has more area' because it 'spreads more'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch. 'L-shape spreads out — true. But Flippy asks — COUNT the tiles in each.'

Guide. Count rectangle: 6. Count L-shape: 6. 'Same number! Area is COUNT of tiles, not how SPREAD OUT.'

More demos. Rearrange 6 tiles into 4 shapes. Count each. All 6.

Generlise. 'Symmy says — area stays the SAME because the COUNT stays the same. Same tiles = same area.'

If still confused: outline both arrangements with a marker on a transparent grid. Count squares inside each outline.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Says spread shapes have more area.
common_misconceptions: Different shape = different area. (Repair: same tiles = same area.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child counts correctly but still says spread = more: transparent-grid overlay; child overlays both arrangements and counts grid cells.
DIAGNOSTIC B — child miscounts tiles: drill 'point and count EVERY tile, no skipping'; chunk in pairs if helpful.
DIAGNOSTIC C — child says rearranging changes area: physical demo — pick up 6 tiles, lay flat, lay tall; child sees same 6 tiles, different shapes.

parts_outline.task: Count tiles in 4 arrangements. Are they all the same area?
Decompose a hexagon into 6 triangles. Show the area is still 6.
Rearrange 8 tiles into 3 different shapes. Show area = 8 each time.
